blocks.content: EXPOSE documents which port an application inside the image is expected to listen on. It is metadata, not a switch that actually opens anything.

EXPOSE 80 tells anyone reading the Dockerfile (and tools that introspect the image) that the application inside listens on port 80. That is genuinely useful documentation, both for humans and for tools like docker run -P that can auto-map exposed ports.

blocks.alt: Documentation of intended ports, built into the image

blocks.content: 2. It Does Not Publish the Port
blocks.text: 2. It Does Not Publish the Port

blocks.content: This is the single most common misunderstanding about EXPOSE: it does not, by itself, make the port reachable from outside the container. Actually publishing a port to the host still requires -p on docker run, exactly as covered in the Port Mapping topic, EXPOSE alone changes nothing about reachability.

blocks.alt: EXPOSE documents, -p is what actually opens the port

blocks.content:
docker run myimage           # port 80 is EXPOSEd but NOT reachable from the host
docker run -p 8080:80 myimage # now it is actually reachable

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: EXPOSE is documentation about which port the application inside listens on, useful metadata, nothing more.
It does not make a port reachable from outside the container, that still requires -p on docker run.
